passage:
I'm Wasim, and I was twenty-two when my daughter Devika turned four. I hovered over her like a kite on a short string. At the colony park I followed her to the slide: "Slow down. Hold the rail. Are you okay?" I wanted to know every bruise and every friend's name.

One evening she pulled her hand out of mine and said, "Papa, I do it." She climbed the ladder alone. I held my breath. She slipped, sat down hard, and looked at me, close to tears. I kept my hands in my pockets and said, "That looked like it hurt. Want to try again?"

She did, and made it to the top.

I saw that most of the fear was mine. Now I ask her one question after school, not ten, and I let some small mistakes stay hers. I still worry, of course.

qa.q: How old was Devika when Wasim was twenty-two?
What was Wasim feeling when Devika slipped, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Fear and the urge to rush in. He held his breath, then kept his hands in his pockets.

qa.q: What changes did Wasim make to how he protects Devika?
qa.a: He asks one question after school instead of ten and lets some small mistakes stay hers, so trust can grow.

qa.q: How might Devika have felt when her father followed her with warnings at the slide?
qa.a: Probably frustrated and held back. Saying "Papa, I do it" shows she wanted to try things by herself.

grounding: A young father who worries and wants to know everything about his child learns that trust grows by letting her make small mistakes.

passage:
Dear Chetan,
Your mother says I should write this instead of saying it badly on the phone, so here it is.
Last month I asked your roommate to tell me when you came back each night, and I checked your location every hour. When your mid-term marks came, I posted them in the family group and wrote, "See what happens in hostel." You haven't really talked to me since.
I was scared. You are nineteen and in a new city, and I kept imagining the worst. But I turned my fear into watching you, and then into shaming you. That was wrong.
From today I have stopped checking your location. I won't contact your roommate. If you mess up a test or come back late sometimes, that is yours to learn from. Tell me what you choose to tell me.
I'm still your Papa. I'll still worry. I'll just try to trust you more than I watch you.
Papa (Naveen)

qa.q: What did Papa post in the family group?
qa.a: Chetan's mid-term marks, with the words "See what happens in hostel."

qa.q: What feeling does Naveen say was behind the watching?
qa.a: Fear: he kept imagining the worst for his nineteen-year-old son in a new city.
To stop checking Chetan's location, stop contacting the roommate, and let Chetan learn from small mistakes.

qa.q: How might Chetan have felt when his marks were posted in the family group?
qa.a: Humiliated and angry, which is why he stopped talking to his father.

grounding: Shows a worried parent who slid into surveillance and shaming, and chooses to build trust by letting the child make small mistakes.

passage:
You asked how I survived Sunaina's first year of college, Farzana? Badly, at first.
She moved into the hostel in Pune, and I called four times a day. I asked for photos of her meals. Once, when she didn't answer for three hours, I called the warden, and her name was announced on the speaker. She was in the library. She didn't talk to me for a week.
Then in October she lost her wallet on the bus: ID card, money, everything. She called me crying, and every part of me wanted to take the next train and fix it. Instead I asked, "What do you think you should do first?" She blocked her card, went to the police post for a report, and borrowed from a friend till the new card came. All by herself.
That's when I understood. My watching wasn't keeping her safe. Her learning was.
I'm Nikita, and I still worry every night. I just call once now.

qa.q: What did Sunaina lose on the bus?
qa.a: Her wallet: ID card, money, everything.

qa.q: What did Nikita feel when Sunaina called crying?
qa.a: Worried and afraid, with a strong urge to rush there and fix everything, which Nikita held back.

qa.q: What did Nikita do instead of fixing the problem?
qa.a: Asked "What do you think you should do first?" and let Sunaina block the card, file the report and borrow from a friend herself.

qa.q: How did Sunaina feel when her name was announced on the speaker?
qa.a: Embarrassed and angry, enough to not speak to her mother for a week.

grounding: Illustrates a protective parent's over-monitoring backfiring, and trust growing once the child handles a small mistake alone.
